newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia invites diplomats, media to northwest.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia invites diplomats, media to northwest.

text.p: Cambodian authorities on Thursday invited diplomats to visit the country's northwest to assess the military situation for themselves after factional clashes in the region earlier this week.
Secretary of State for Information Khieu Kanarith said the envoys and some reporters would travel to the northwest city of Battambang and the northern town of Siem Reap.
"Military attaches and also some reporters can go to Batambang and Siem Reap today to check the situation there," he said.
It was not clear which countries' representatives would be asked along on the flight.
Earlier this week, there were clashes in both areas between forces loyal to deposed First Prime Minster Prince Norodom Ranariddh and those under powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
The clashes broke out shortly after Hun Sen's troops took the capital Phnom Penh at the weekend in what Ranariddh described as a coup.
Ranariddh's forces have traditionally had more strength in and controlled, those northwestern Cambodian areas.
Cambodia's U.N. ambassador, a Ranariddh loyalist, said on Wednesday in New York that Ranariddh's supporters would amass troops in Battambang and set up an alternative regime.
"We will take Battambang, the second city. We have disarmed more than 2,000 (opposing) soldiers," the ambassador, Prince Sisowath Sirirath, told a news conference in New York.
"This is our home and we will have a capital city...," he said, adding that Battambang would be declared "a city for the national resistence."
Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh on Sunday after two days of heavy fighting in the capital. The prince had left the country on the eve of the fighting last Friday.

A military official in Battambang said on Thursday it was quiet and that the road to the Thai border to the west was open as usual. Earlier in the week sources in the north had said the road had been mined.

Two of Cambodia's southeast Asian neighbours, the Philippines and Malaysia, were expected to fly more planes into the capital to evacuate their nationals while commercial flights to and from Phnom Penh were gradually returning to normal, an aviation official in the capital said.
The Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore all sent special planes to the capital on Wednesday to evacuate hundreds of their citizens.
Four flights were due between Phnom Penh and Ho Chi Minh City in southern Vietnam on Thursday, Keo Sophal, secretary general of the Civil Aviation Department told Reuters.
Two Royal Air Cambodge flights to Bangkok were also scheduled as well as another five chartered flights to the Thai capital, he said.
But the Malaysian and Thai flag carriers were not scheduled to resume services today, he said.
Phnom Phen's airport was heavily damaged over the two days of fighting and a third day of looting.
"It is a little bit difficult for passengers because they cannot yet restore the passenger building and are checking people in outside," Keo Sophal said.

He also said a military transport plane would fly from the Thai military airport at U-Tapao southeast of Bangkok to Siem Reap to evacuate people from the tourist town which is home to the 12th century Angkor Wat ruins.
The United States said on Wednesday it was pulling about 40 diplomats and their dependents out of Cambodia but would keep the mission open.

An official at the embassy in Phnom Penh said the U.S. diplomats were not due to begin leaving on Thursday but said some U.S. citizens were hoping to leaving the city in the morning on one of the charter flights.
